idiom_name: generator function (yield) as a seed-driven unfold
implementation_notes: Python absorbs the generator: any def containing yield is a generator function (PEP 255) that returns a generator iterator suspending at each yield, so seed, step and stop condition are ordinary local variables and the caller pulls with next() or for. The standard library ships no unfold combinator; where the step function should be a first-class value, a five-line driver reproduces the scheme, and itertools supplies the consumer side (islice/takewhile to bound, chain/accumulate to combine). Tree unfolds are recursive builders (dataclasses plus an explicit stack) because the generator protocol only linearises a traversal.
code_sketch:
def unfold(seed, step):            # step: S -> (value, next_seed) | None
    while (r := step(seed)) is not None:
        yield r[0]                 # one layer per next()
        seed = r[1]

from itertools import islice
list(islice(unfold(8, lambda n: (n, n // 2) if n > 1 else None), 3))   # [8, 4, 2]
pitfalls: A generator is single-use and holds its frame: an exhausted one raises StopIteration forever, and an abandoned one keeps its locals (and any open resource) alive until collection.
Deep recursive construction hits the interpreter recursion limit long before memory does; use an explicit stack for input-driven depth.
Closures and default arguments capture the seed by reference, so rebinding the outer name changes a generator that has not finished.
